The sky appears blue because of a process called Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight, which looks white, is actually a mixture of all visible colors, each with a different wavelength. When this light enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with tiny gas molecules like nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of light—blue and violet—far more effectively than longer wavelengths like red and orange. Because blue light is scattered in all directions across the sky and reaches our eyes from every part of the atmosphere, the sky takes on a blue hue. Violet is scattered even more than blue, but our eyes are less sensitive to violet, and some of it is absorbed by the upper atmosphere, so the sky reads as blue to the human eye. At sunset, the light travels through a longer path of atmosphere, scattering away most of the blue and leaving the warmer reds and oranges we associate with twilight.

This is the classic explanation for the blue sky. Let me make sure it's accurate and complete:

- Sunlight is white (all visible wavelengths)
- Enters atmosphere, hits gas molecules
- Rayleigh scattering: intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength (∝ 1/λ⁴)
- Shorter wavelengths (blue ~450nm) scatter much more than longer ones (red ~650nm)
- Violet (~400nm) scatters even more, but human eye less sensitive to violet, and some is absorbed by ozone
- Net result: sky appears blue

The paragraph covers all the key points clearly and concisely. Good.
